title: Sorting & Limiting
subtitle: ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET, and pagination
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Rows come back in undefined order (the database picks whatever is fastest). You need results in a meaningful order — cheapest first, newest first, alphabetical.
whyItExists.solution: ORDER BY sorts results. LIMIT caps the number of rows. OFFSET skips rows for pagination. Together they power every sorted list and paginated result in an app.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any time result order matters to the user. Any time you only need the top-N results. Pagination in APIs and UIs.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't use ORDER BY + LIMIT for finding a 'random' row at scale — it forces a full sort. Use ORDER BY RANDOM() LIMIT 1 (SQLite) or TABLESAMPLE (PostgreSQL) for random sampling.

explainModes.beginner: ORDER BY sorts the results. ORDER BY price sorts cheapest first (ASC). ORDER BY price DESC sorts most expensive first. LIMIT 5 returns only 5 rows. OFFSET 10 skips the first 10 rows — useful for page 2, 3, etc.
explainModes.simple: ORDER BY col ASC (default, A→Z, 0→9) or DESC. Multiple sort keys: ORDER BY category ASC, price DESC. LIMIT n — return n rows. OFFSET n — skip first n rows. LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20 — rows 21-30 (page 3 of 10). NULLs sort last in ASC, first in DESC in PostgreSQL; use NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST.
explainModes.standard: ORDER BY is the last operation (after WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT). Column aliases from SELECT can be used in ORDER BY — unlike WHERE. ORDER BY column_position: ORDER BY 2 sorts by the second column (fragile, avoid in code). Without ORDER BY, row order is non-deterministic even for the same query. For stable pagination, ORDER BY must include a unique column.
explainModes.technical: Sorting is expensive — O(n log n). The engine may use an index to avoid sorting if the ORDER BY matches an index. For LIMIT/OFFSET pagination, the engine still evaluates all earlier rows — OFFSET 10000 is as slow as fetching 10000 rows. Keyset/cursor pagination (WHERE id > last_seen_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 10) is O(log n) with an index. Covering indexes include all SELECT columns — no heap lookup needed.
explainModes.deepDive: OFFSET pagination has O(n) cost for deep pages — row 1,000,001 requires reading 1,000,001 rows then discarding the first million. Keyset pagination solves this: remember the last id/timestamp and use it in WHERE. Row_number() window function enables stable page extraction without OFFSET. FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY WITH TIES returns additional rows with the same value as the nth row.

questions.question: What does LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10 return?
options: A random 5 rows from the table
questions.explanation: OFFSET skips rows first, then LIMIT takes from there. LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10 skips the first 10 rows and returns the next 5 (rows 11-15). This is page 3 with a page size of 5.

faq.q: Does the row order matter without ORDER BY?
faq.a: Yes — without ORDER BY, the database can return rows in any order it wants. It might be consistent today but change after an index rebuild or table update. Never depend on row order without an explicit ORDER BY.

faq.q: What is wrong with OFFSET for deep pagination?
faq.a: OFFSET 100000 still causes the database to process 100,000 rows before skipping them — it's O(n) for the offset. Keyset pagination (WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 10) uses the index and is always O(log n). Use keyset for large datasets.

examples: SELECT * FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET ?  — paginated blog feed
SELECT user_id, SUM(total) FROM orders GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY SUM(total) DESC LIMIT 10 — top 10 customers
SELECT * FROM events ORDER BY id WHERE id > ? LIMIT 50 — keyset pagination
